stem: A 74-year-old with LVEF 25% presents with orthopnoea, bilateral crackles, JVP elevation and pitting oedema. BP is 158/92 mmHg, HR 94/min, SpO2 91% on room air. He is alert with warm extremities and no chest pain.
ask: Which immediate management is MOST appropriate?
options: Give a rapid 2-litre IV crystalloid bolus to improve cardiac output.
Stop all diuretics and give an IV beta blocker to lower the pulse immediately.
Begin IV loop diuretic, titrated oxygen if hypoxaemic, and monitor renal function, electrolytes and diuresis.
Proceed to immediate inotropic infusion despite normal peripheral perfusion and elevated BP.
Treat presumed pneumonia with antibiotics alone before considering fluid removal.
explanations: He is clinically congested and not hypoperfused; a large bolus would worsen pulmonary oedema.
Acute decompensated congestion needs decongestion first; IV beta blockade may cause deterioration.
Correct: a warm, wet patient with high BP and fluid overload needs decongestion and reassessment.
Inotropes are for selected low-output/hypoperfused states, not routine hypertensive congestion.
Crackles plus elevated JVP, oedema and HFrEF support cardiogenic congestion; infection can coexist but does not replace diuresis.
pearl: Classify acute heart failure by congestion (wet/dry) and perfusion (warm/cold) before choosing diuretics, vasodilators, fluids or inotropes.
pivot: If hypotensive, cold and oliguric, consider cardiogenic shock with urgent critical-care, echocardiography and vasoactive support.

steps: Stabilise
Sit upright, continuous saturation/ECG, oxygen only as needed; assess chest pain, arrhythmia and respiratory fatigue.
Decongest
IV loop diuretic, strict fluid balance and urine output; consider nitrates if markedly hypertensive and appropriate.
Investigate
ECG, troponin when indicated, chest radiograph/ultrasound, renal function, electrolytes, BNP as useful; echocardiography.
Reassess
BP, dyspnoea, weight, urine, potassium and creatinine; optimise guideline-directed chronic therapy once stable.
management.safety: Avoid nitrates in significant hypotension and aggressive diuresis without assessing perfusion and renal response.
management.local: Exam teaching framework. Confirm drug doses, contraindications and treatment thresholds with current local protocols and supervising teams.

stem: A 34-year-old multiparous woman delivers the fetal head, which retracts tightly against the perineum. Gentle axial traction fails and the anterior shoulder is not delivering. CTG before head delivery was reassuring.
ask: Which immediate manoeuvres are MOST appropriate?
options: Apply strong downward traction on the fetal head while an assistant gives fundal pressure.
Wait five minutes before intervening because shoulder dystocia often resolves spontaneously.
Perform an episiotomy alone to free the bony shoulder impaction.
Call for help, use McRoberts positioning and suprapubic pressure while avoiding fundal pressure.
Immediately perform emergency Caesarean section after the fetal head has delivered.
explanations: Excessive traction risks brachial plexus injury; fundal pressure can worsen impaction.
Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency; prolonged head-to-body interval increases hypoxia risk.
Episiotomy may create space for internal manoeuvres but does not release a shoulder trapped behind symphysis.
Correct: these are first-line actions for recognised shoulder dystocia.
Routine Caesarean is not an appropriate first manoeuvre after head delivery; bedside shoulder dystocia techniques are urgent.
pearl: Shoulder dystocia is defined by failure of shoulders to deliver with routine gentle traction; McRoberts and suprapubic pressure are initial manoeuvres.
pivot: If initial external manoeuvres fail, consider internal rotation, posterior arm delivery or all-fours position under skilled assistance.

steps: Call and record
Announce shoulder dystocia, call obstetric/neonatal help and record time of head delivery.
Release impaction
McRoberts hyperflexion and correctly directed suprapubic pressure; no fundal pressure, no forceful traction.
Next manoeuvres
Senior-led internal rotation or posterior arm delivery if needed; call anaesthesia/theatre backup.
After birth
Neonatal examination for brachial plexus injury/fracture, manage PPH/perineal injury and debrief/document.
management.safety: A routine episiotomy does not fix bony shoulder impaction.
management.local: Clinical teaching only. Use the relevant maternity/neonatal/paediatric escalation pathway and current local drug/weight-based protocols.

stem: A 61-year-old on day 4 after total hip replacement develops sudden pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia 126/min and SpO2 90% on room air. BP is 122/78 mmHg. He has no fever, chest auscultation is clear and no contraindication to CTPA is known.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate next investigation/action?
options: Treat as atelectasis without testing because hypoxia is common after surgery.
Obtain a D-dimer only and exclude PE if it is normal.
Give empirical therapeutic anticoagulation blindly without considering surgical bleeding or diagnostics.
Arrange urgent CTPA with monitoring and parallel senior review of anticoagulation/bleeding risk.
Perform exercise stress testing before imaging for embolism.
explanations: Sudden pleuritic pain, tachycardia and hypoxaemia with VTE risk warrant urgent PE assessment.
Postoperative D-dimer is frequently elevated and may be inappropriate/insufficient for this high-risk setting.
Treatment may be started if strongly suspected and imaging delayed, but recent surgery requires bleeding-risk assessment and senior input.
Correct: a stable patient with suspected significant PE can undergo definitive vascular imaging promptly.
Exertional testing is inappropriate during acute hypoxaemic pleuritic symptoms.
pearl: PE clinical probability and patient stability determine imaging and empirical anticoagulation decisions; recent surgery complicates bleeding risk.
pivot: If hypotensive or too unstable for CT, use bedside echo/critical-care PE pathway and consider urgent reperfusion.

steps: Initial
ABCDE, oxygen to target, IV access, ECG, troponin/BNP if risk stratification indicated; discuss recent surgery/bleeding.
Diagnose
CTPA promptly if stable; compression ultrasound if relevant and alternative imaging in contraindication.
Treat
Start therapeutic anticoagulation when confirmed or high probability with acceptable bleeding risk, with orthopaedic/medical consultation.
Monitor
Oxygenation, haemodynamics and RV strain; escalate rapidly if BP falls.
management.safety: Recent spinal/neuraxial anaesthesia and surgery may influence anticoagulant timing and choice.
management.local: Apply current hospital antibiotics, imaging, procedural and anticoagulation guidance with surgical and critical-care supervision.

context: Advanced psychiatry primary care and medication safety
stem: A 23-year-old previously well student has three days of bizarre behaviour, agitation and persecutory ideas. Today she has fever 38.8 °C, severe headache, episodic confusion and a new focal seizure. Family confirms this is her first psychiatric presentation.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate immediate response?
options: Diagnose schizophrenia based on persecutory content and arrange routine outpatient medication review.
Give an antipsychotic and discharge when her speech becomes calmer.
Admit for urgent medical/neurological assessment and begin indicated empiric encephalitis/meningitis treatment without unsafe delay.
Perform psychological testing over several weeks before ordering blood tests or imaging.
Perform lumbar puncture immediately without considering imaging or seizure-related contraindications.
explanations: Abrupt onset, fever, seizure and fluctuating consciousness are red flags for neurological/infectious causes.
Sedation does not treat meningitis/encephalitis or secure safety after seizure.
Correct: new psychosis with fever and seizure warrants emergency evaluation for infectious, autoimmune or metabolic encephalopathy.
Neuroinfection and seizure are time-critical; psychometric assessment is not the priority.
LP is important when safe, but clinical signs may require imaging and stabilization; treatment must not wait.
pearl: New-onset psychotic symptoms with altered consciousness, focal neurological signs, fever or seizures should be considered organic until assessed.
pivot: Chronic stable psychotic symptoms without physical/neurological red flags may follow a usual first-episode psychosis assessment pathway.

steps: Stabilise
ABCDE, seizure management, temperature, bedside glucose, IV access and continuous observation.
Investigate
FBC/CRP, UEC/glucose/toxicology as relevant, cultures, urgent neuroimaging when indicated and LP when safe.
Treat early
Empiric IV aciclovir if encephalitis suspected plus meningitis antibiotics when clinically indicated; liaise ID/neurology/psychiatry.
Protect patient
Assess behavioural and seizure risk; use least restrictive supportive measures and monitor cognition.
management.safety: Do not let psychiatric labels delay consideration of HSV encephalitis or anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.
management.local: Educational safety guide: confirm treatment and statutory reporting with your local specialist guidelines and safeguarding law.

stem: A 63-year-old has crushing inferior chest pain with ST elevation in II, III and aVF. BP is 82/50 mmHg, JVP is raised and lungs are clear. Right-sided ECG leads show ST elevation in V4R. He received no nitrates yet.
ask: Which immediate management plan is MOST appropriate?
options: Administer sublingual GTN every 5 minutes to reduce preload and relieve pain.
Activate reperfusion and support RV preload cautiously while avoiding nitrates; involve cardiology urgently.
Give IV furosemide as first-line therapy because elevated JVP confirms pulmonary congestion.
Delay reperfusion to obtain serial troponin levels for confirmation.
Start high-dose beta blocker immediately despite shock.
explanations: RV infarction is preload-dependent; nitrates can precipitate profound hypotension.
Correct: RV STEMI needs timely reperfusion, thoughtful haemodynamic support and avoiding preload-reducing drugs.
High JVP here reflects RV failure with clear lungs; diuresis can worsen low cardiac output.
An ECG-confirmed STEMI requires urgent activation, not serial biomarker delay.
Negative inotropy can worsen hypotension in acute RV infarction.
pearl: Inferior STEMI with hypotension, elevated JVP and clear lungs suggests RV involvement: avoid nitrates and unconsidered diuresis.
pivot: If pulmonary oedema and hypertension predominate instead, nitrates and diuretics may be useful with appropriate monitoring.

steps: Urgent cardiac pathway
ECG including right-sided leads, resuscitation monitoring and direct activation of primary PCI.
Support perfusion
Assess for hypovolaemia and cautiously consider small IV fluid boluses if appropriate, repeated reassessment; senior vasopressor support if shock persists.
Reperfuse and monitor
Protocol-directed aspirin/antithrombotic therapy, PCI, serial ECG and watch for AV block/arrhythmias.
management.safety: Excessive fluid may also harm an infarcted RV; use bedside assessment rather than automatic large boluses.
management.local: Exam teaching framework. Confirm drug doses, contraindications and treatment thresholds with current local protocols and supervising teams.

stem: A 29-year-old with a prior low-transverse Caesarean is in induced labour at 39 weeks. She develops sudden constant abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, BP 88/54 mmHg and fetal bradycardia at 65/min. The presenting part is now higher on vaginal examination.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate next action?
options: Stop oxytocin, activate an emergency obstetric response, resuscitate and proceed urgently to laparotomy/birth.
Increase oxytocin because labour progress appears to have arrested.
Perform fetal scalp stimulation and observe for thirty minutes.
Provide tocolysis and schedule elective Caesarean after the following morning ward round.
Give oral analgesia and reassure that scar stretching commonly causes severe pain.
explanations: Correct: uterine rupture is highly probable and needs immediate maternal resuscitation and surgical delivery.
More uterotonic stimulation may worsen rupture and haemorrhage.
Persistent severe bradycardia with maternal instability demands intervention, not diagnostic delay.
A ruptured uterus with shock requires immediate theatre and blood preparation.
Pain plus fetal collapse and loss of station is not normal scar stretching.
pearl: New pain, fetal bradycardia and loss of presenting-part station during VBAC are classic rupture red flags.
pivot: With an intact uterus but uncomplicated uterine tachysystole and reassuring fetus, oxytocin reduction and conservative measures may suffice.

steps: Immediate response
Stop oxytocin, call consultant obstetrics/anaesthetics/neonatal and activate massive haemorrhage support.
Resuscitate
ABCDE, large-bore access, bloods/crossmatch, blood products, oxygen if hypoxaemic, maternal left tilt.
Operate
Emergency laparotomy and delivery; repair versus hysterectomy depending extent and haemostasis.
Aftercare
Post-haemorrhage/ICU monitoring, counselling about future pregnancy risks.
management.safety: Do not delay surgery for confirmatory ultrasound if clinical rupture and fetal compromise are clear.
management.local: Clinical teaching only. Use the relevant maternity/neonatal/paediatric escalation pathway and current local drug/weight-based protocols.

skill: Necrotising soft tissue infection / source control
stem: A 55-year-old with diabetes has rapidly progressive leg pain two days after a small cut. Pain is far worse than surface erythema; there is purple mottling, bullae, fever 39.2 °C, BP 86/48 mmHg and lactate 5.0. Crepitus is absent.
ask: Which is the BEST management?
options: Give oral flucloxacillin and mark the erythema margin for review tomorrow.
Start resuscitation, urgent broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and immediate surgical exploration/debridement.
Order MRI and defer antibiotics until imaging precisely defines fascial necrosis.
Use topical antiseptic dressings and observe for development of crepitus.
Give corticosteroids to treat the intense pain and local swelling.
explanations: Shock and pain out of proportion indicate potential necrotising infection; outpatient antibiotics are unsafe.
Correct: necrotising fasciitis is a surgical source-control emergency; imaging should not delay surgery when suspicion is high.
MRI can be helpful in uncertain stable cases but should not delay antibiotics or exploration in shock.
Absence of crepitus does not exclude necrotising infection; delay allows rapid progression.
Steroids are not definitive treatment and may worsen infection without source control.
pearl: Pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity and rapidly evolving skin signs are early necrotising fasciitis clues even without gas.
pivot: Uncomplicated cellulitis without systemic toxicity or deep pain can be treated with appropriate antibiotics and follow-up.

steps: Recognise / mobilise
Sepsis resuscitation, call general/orthopaedic/plastic surgery plus ICU immediately.
Treat
Broad IV coverage for Gram-positive, Gram-negative and anaerobic bacteria, with antitoxin agent where toxin-mediated streptococcal infection suspected.
Operate
Urgent extensive debridement and repeat theatre assessments; imaging only if it does not delay source control.
Monitor
Lactate, renal function, shock support, wound cultures and antibiotic tailoring.
management.safety: Do not wait for crepitus, high LRINEC score or normal skin to declare the process safe.
management.local: Apply current hospital antibiotics, imaging, procedural and anticoagulation guidance with surgical and critical-care supervision.

context: Advanced psychiatry primary care and medication safety
stem: A 24-year-old has slept under two hours nightly for nine days, is excessively talkative, has spent her savings on a 'global media company' and believes her television is communicating directly with her. She is agitated and refuses food. No illicit substances detected.
ask: Which immediate management is MOST appropriate?
options: Start an SSRI antidepressant to reduce irritability and review in six weeks.
Discharge because high energy without sadness excludes a mood episode.
Treat with psychotherapy alone because medication will affect creativity.
Assess risk and capacity, arrange acute psychiatric care and initiate an antipsychotic with mood-stabilising strategy as clinically indicated.
Diagnose hypomania because she remains able to articulate her ideas.
explanations: Antidepressant monotherapy can worsen mania and does not address acute psychosis and impaired judgment.
Severe impairment, psychosis, reduced sleep and risky spending indicate mania needing urgent assessment.
Therapy may be useful later, but acute severe mania generally needs medication and safe supervision.
Correct: severe mania with psychotic features and self-neglect requires urgent containment, sleep restoration and pharmacotherapy.
Psychosis or marked functional impairment meets mania, not hypomania; communication ability does not downgrade severity.
pearl: Mania is a mood episode with marked impairment or psychosis; psychotic features automatically exclude hypomania.
pivot: A shorter elevated mood period without marked impairment or psychosis may represent hypomania, affecting the bipolar subtype.

steps: Assess
Risk to self/others, food/fluid intake, sleep deprivation, finances, substance use, medical causes and decision capacity.
Stabilise
Low-stimulation supervised setting; short-term antipsychotic with adjunct benzodiazepine as needed and mood stabiliser strategy under psychiatry.
Monitor
ECG, metabolic profile, pregnancy status and medication risks; restore nutrition/hydration and sleep.
Plan follow-up
Psychoeducation, early relapse signals, adherence and family engagement with consent.
management.safety: Lithium, valproate and antipsychotic selection require pregnancy/reproductive counselling and monitoring.
management.local: Educational safety guide: confirm treatment and statutory reporting with your local specialist guidelines and safeguarding law.

stem: A 28-year-old presents with sudden palpitations. Monitor shows regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 184/min. She is alert, BP 126/74 mmHg, no chest pain and SpO2 99%. No known structural heart disease or asthma.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate first active treatment?
options: Immediate unsynchronised defibrillation at cardiac-arrest energy.
Give IV amiodarone as first-line before trying non-pharmacological measures.
Give oral verapamil immediately without IV access or rhythm reassessment.
Perform a modified Valsalva manoeuvre with ECG monitoring, then use IV adenosine if unsuccessful.
Give therapeutic anticoagulation because all narrow-complex tachycardia is atrial fibrillation.
explanations: She has a pulse and is stable; unsynchronised shock is not first-line for stable SVT.
Amiodarone is not first-line for uncomplicated stable regular narrow-complex SVT.
Calcium-channel blockers may have a role but vagal measures and monitored adenosine are usual first steps.
Correct: vagal manoeuvres are preferred first active therapy in stable regular AV-node-dependent SVT.
Regular narrow tachycardia differs from AF; anticoagulation does not terminate SVT.
pearl: Management of tachyarrhythmia begins with haemodynamic stability and QRS width/regularity, not simply the heart rate.
pivot: If shock, ischaemic chest pain or pulmonary oedema develops, synchronised cardioversion becomes urgent.

steps: Check stability
ABCDE, IV access and 12-lead ECG; look for pre-excitation, wide QRS or irregular rhythm.
Try vagal therapy
Modified Valsalva with supine reposition and leg raise where appropriate.
If persistent
Rapid IV adenosine via proximal cannula with flush and continuous ECG if rhythm suitable; prepare for transient AV block and discuss contraindications.
Escalate
Alternative drugs or synchronised cardioversion under specialist guidance if refractory or unstable.
management.safety: Avoid AV-nodal blockers for irregular wide-complex pre-excited AF; assess rhythm carefully before adenosine.
management.local: Exam teaching framework. Confirm drug doses, contraindications and treatment thresholds with current local protocols and supervising teams.

stem: A 28-year-old on postoperative day 3 after emergency Caesarean develops temperature 39 °C, tachycardia, uterine fundal tenderness and foul-smelling lochia. Incision is clean and there is no respiratory or urinary complaint.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate treatment?
options: Give oral metronidazole alone and discharge because foul lochia is normal after Caesarean.
Begin IV broad-spectrum antibiotics covering anaerobes and genital tract organisms with sepsis assessment.
Arrange immediate hysterectomy before giving antimicrobials.
Withhold all antibiotics until an endometrial swab culture results.
Give a short course of oral antifungal medication for presumed candida vaginitis.
explanations: This is clinically consistent with postpartum endometritis; broad IV therapy and observation are usually needed.
Correct: post-Caesarean endometritis is polymicrobial and should be treated promptly with broad IV coverage.
Surgery is reserved for refractory infection/complications, not uncomplicated endometritis.
Endometritis is diagnosed clinically and prompt empiric therapy reduces morbidity.
Yeast infection does not explain high fever, uterine tenderness and systemic tachycardia.
pearl: Postpartum endometritis is often diagnosed clinically from fever, uterine tenderness and abnormal lochia, particularly post-Caesarean.
pivot: If fever persists despite adequate therapy, evaluate retained products, abscess, septic pelvic thrombophlebitis or another source.

steps: Assess severity
Vital signs, sepsis screen, abdominal and wound examination, blood cultures if septic, FBC, renal function and lactate as indicated.
Treat promptly
IV broad-spectrum antibiotics with anaerobic coverage (e.g. locally approved clindamycin–gentamicin regimen or alternative), plus fluids and analgesia.
Reassess
Monitor fever, haemodynamics and uterine tenderness; consider ultrasound if retained tissue/abscess suspected.
Escalate
Senior O&G review and source control if refractory or complicated infection.
management.safety: Choice of antibiotics depends on allergy, renal function, antimicrobial guidance and breastfeeding considerations.
management.local: Clinical teaching only. Use the relevant maternity/neonatal/paediatric escalation pathway and current local drug/weight-based protocols.

stem: A 47-year-old taking frequent NSAIDs develops sudden severe epigastric pain followed by a rigid, diffusely tender abdomen. Upright chest X-ray shows free subdiaphragmatic air. BP 96/58 mmHg and pulse 118/min.
ask: Which management is MOST appropriate?
options: Give a PPI and observe for 48 hours because NSAID ulcers often heal spontaneously.
Perform colonoscopy to locate the defect before operative referral.
Treat with oral Helicobacter pylori eradication alone and discharge.
Give analgesia only until hypotension becomes more severe, then arrange imaging.
NPO, resuscitate with IV fluids/antibiotics and PPI, and obtain urgent operative review for perforation repair.
explanations: Peritonitis and free air signal perforation needing urgent surgical source control.
Endoscopy can worsen insufflation/perforation and delays emergency treatment.
Eradication treats underlying infection later; it does not seal a free perforation in peritonitis.
Immediate resuscitation and surgery are necessary before further shock progression.
Correct: treat sepsis/peritoneal contamination and obtain definitive surgical control.
pearl: Free intraperitoneal air plus generalised peritonitis is a surgical emergency; resuscitation and antibiotics happen before and during theatre.
pivot: A small sealed perforation in a stable carefully selected patient may have non-operative management under specialist observation.

steps: First response
ABCDE, call surgical and anaesthetic teams, NPO, IV lines, bloods/crossmatch and fluid resuscitation.
Prevent progression
Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics for enteric contamination, IV PPI, nasogastric decompression where indicated.
Definitive control
Urgent surgery for closure/repair and peritoneal washout; H. pylori/NSAID risk treatment after recovery.
Follow
Sepsis, leak, renal function and postoperative nutrition monitoring.
management.safety: Avoid delays from unnecessary investigations when imaging already shows free air and clinical peritonitis.
management.local: Apply current hospital antibiotics, imaging, procedural and anticoagulation guidance with surgical and critical-care supervision.

context: Advanced psychiatry primary care and medication safety
stem: A 38-year-old with schizophrenia is admitted after abruptly becoming mute and motionless for 18 hours. She maintains unusual postures and exhibits waxy flexibility and negativism. Temp 36.8 °C, HR 88/min and CK normal. She is not eating or drinking.
ask: What is the BEST immediate treatment approach?
options: Perform a monitored lorazepam challenge while checking medical complications and planning ECT if refractory.
Increase high-potency antipsychotic dose immediately until she starts speaking.
Interpret the mutism as deliberate refusal and withdraw fluid support.
Use physical restraints continuously without medical evaluation.
Give a stimulant such as methylphenidate as sole initial treatment.
explanations: Correct: benzodiazepines are first-line for catatonia; failure or severe illness may need ECT.
Antipsychotic escalation can worsen catatonia and precipitate malignant catatonia/NMS in some situations.
Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric syndrome with dehydration, thrombosis and rhabdomyolysis risks.
Restraints may cause injury and do not treat the syndrome; least-restrictive care and medical protection are needed.
Psychostimulants are not standard first-line treatment for catatonia.
pearl: Recognise mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility and negativism as catatonia; assess hydration, immobility complications and underlying cause.
pivot: Fever, autonomic instability and CK rise raise concern for malignant catatonia or neuroleptic malignant syndrome with immediate ICU/ECT pathways.

steps: Assess
Urgent psychiatry and medical review, catatonia scale, medication history, neurological signs and differential incl NMS/encephalitis.
Treat
Monitored lorazepam challenge followed by scheduled benzodiazepine if responsive; plan ECT for nonresponse or severe case.
Prevent harm
IV/NG fluids/nutrition as needed, VTE prophylaxis when appropriate, pressure care and monitoring for infection/CK elevation.
Reassess drugs
Review dopamine antagonists and other precipitants with psychiatry.
management.safety: Do not escalate antipsychotics reflexively in active catatonia; malignant catatonia needs urgent specialist treatment.
management.local: Educational safety guide: confirm treatment and statutory reporting with your local specialist guidelines and safeguarding law.

stem: A 67-year-old with severe hypertension develops sudden dyspnoea and pink frothy sputum. BP 206/112 mmHg, RR 36/min, SpO2 80% despite nasal oxygen, diffuse crackles and marked distress. He remains conscious and cooperative.
ask: Which immediate strategy is MOST appropriate?
options: Begin non-invasive positive-pressure ventilation with urgent BP reduction (e.g. nitrates if suitable) and cardiac monitoring.
Give 2 L crystalloid immediately before treating BP because tachypnoea causes volume depletion.
Provide only oral diuretic medication and review saturation in two hours.
Give morphine routinely as the first and most important treatment.
Wait for a formal echocardiogram before offering positive-pressure ventilation.
explanations: Correct: hypertensive cardiogenic pulmonary oedema needs rapid oxygenation/ventilatory support and afterload reduction.
Fluids worsen already flooded alveoli and impaired gas exchange.
Oral diuresis is too slow for severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure.
Routine opiates can cause respiratory depression and hypotension; they are not first-line rescue therapy.
Bedside physiology supports immediate treatment; echocardiography should not delay stabilisation.
pearl: In acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema with severe hypertension, NIV plus rapidly acting vasodilators may relieve distress quickly while diuresis removes excess fluid.
pivot: If severely hypotensive with cool peripheries, avoid nitrates and manage potential cardiogenic shock with critical-care input.

steps: Support airway/breathing
Sit upright, urgent team response, oxygen and CPAP/BiPAP if suitable; prepare intubation if exhaustion or contraindications.
Reduce afterload and congestion
Titrated nitrates if BP supports it and IV loop diuretic where overloaded; avoid routine opioids.
Find triggers
ECG/troponin, arrhythmia, BP, chest imaging, renal function and echo; reassess cardiogenic versus non-cardiogenic cause.
Monitor
Frequent SpO2, RR, consciousness, BP and urine output.
management.safety: NIV requires monitoring and cooperation; altered consciousness, inability to protect airway or worsening shock may mandate intubation.
management.local: Exam teaching framework. Confirm drug doses, contraindications and treatment thresholds with current local protocols and supervising teams.

stem: A 33-year-old at 31 weeks presents with painless bright-red vaginal bleeding. She has no contractions, BP 120/76 mmHg and fetal heart rate is reassuring. A scan at 20 weeks showed a low-lying anterior placenta.
ask: Which immediate assessment is MOST appropriate?
options: Perform a digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilation before imaging.
Induce labour immediately because any bleeding in late pregnancy requires vaginal delivery.
Discharge without assessment because painless bleeding always settles.
Perform speculum examination only after excluding placenta praevia by digital palpation.
Assess maternal and fetal stability and use ultrasound to locate placenta before any digital vaginal examination.
explanations: Digital examination risks catastrophic haemorrhage if placenta praevia overlies the os.
Delivery planning depends on bleeding severity, gestation, placental location and fetal/maternal status.
A third-trimester bleed warrants evaluation and observation depending on amount/risk.
Digital palpation itself is contraindicated; ultrasound should establish placental location.
Correct: suspected placenta praevia requires safe evaluation without digital vaginal exam.
pearl: Painless antepartum bleeding with prior low placenta suggests placenta praevia until proven otherwise: NO digital vaginal exam.
pivot: Painful bleeding with a tender hypertonic uterus suggests placental abruption, which may have concealed blood loss.

steps: Stabilise
Maternal ABC, vitals, amount of bleeding, IV access/crossmatch if needed and fetal CTG assessment.
Confirm location
Transabdominal and/or transvaginal ultrasound safely determines placental relation to cervix.
Plan care
Senior obstetric review; anti-D when indicated, antenatal steroids if preterm birth risk and timing/location of delivery based on ongoing bleeding.
management.safety: Never perform digital vaginal exam in suspected placenta praevia before imaging.
management.local: Clinical teaching only. Use the relevant maternity/neonatal/paediatric escalation pathway and current local drug/weight-based protocols.

stem: A 49-year-old with alcohol-related acute pancreatitis has persistent abdominal pain and raised inflammatory markers on day 4. CT shows pancreatic necrosis but no gas in collections. She is afebrile, haemodynamically stable and has no cultures suggesting infection.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Commence broad IV antibiotics solely because CT demonstrates sterile necrosis.
Perform early necrosectomy in all necrotising cases to reduce inflammatory markers.
Continue supportive care, early nutrition as tolerated and vigilant surveillance without routine prophylactic antibiotics.
Keep the patient nil by mouth for two weeks to rest the pancreas.
Give prophylactic antifungals to prevent future pancreatic infection.
explanations: Prophylactic antibiotics do not prevent infected pancreatic necrosis and are not routinely indicated.
Early surgery in sterile necrosis causes harm; intervention is reserved for infected or symptomatic complications when feasible delayed.
Correct: sterile necrosis needs organ support and monitoring, not routine antimicrobial treatment.
Early enteral/oral nutrition as tolerated reduces complications compared with prolonged starvation.
Routine antifungal prophylaxis is not supported absent specific infection/high-risk circumstances.
pearl: Pancreatic necrosis can be sterile. Treat infected necrosis with antibiotics and appropriately timed drainage/source control, but do not prophylax sterile tissue.
pivot: If gas, bacteraemia, sepsis or clinical deterioration suggests infected necrosis, start targeted antibiotics and discuss step-up drainage.

steps: Assess complications
Serial clinical observations and organ function, fluid/electrolyte balance and severity scores; ICU if organ failure.
Support
Judicious fluids, adequate analgesia, early oral/enteral nutrition as tolerated and thromboprophylaxis when safe.
Monitor infection
Look for fever, gas in collection, bacteraemia or new organ dysfunction; delay invasive intervention for sterile stable necrosis.
Escalate
Multidisciplinary step-up drainage/necrosectomy for infected or symptomatic collections.
management.safety: Routine prophylactic carbapenems and early necrosectomy are not indicated in stable sterile necrosis.
management.local: Apply current hospital antibiotics, imaging, procedural and anticoagulation guidance with surgical and critical-care supervision.

context: Advanced psychiatry primary care and medication safety
stem: A 27-year-old reports sudden distressing images of harming her baby, which she finds abhorrent and inconsistent with her beliefs. She avoids knives and repeatedly seeks reassurance. She has never wanted to harm the infant, recognises thoughts are her own and has no hallucinations or fixed delusions.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Diagnose infanticidal psychosis and arrange compulsory admission solely because she describes an image of harm.
Offer CBT with exposure and response prevention, consider an SSRI and assess actual risk/functional impairment.
Prescribe antipsychotic monotherapy without psychological treatment because all harm thoughts are delusions.
Advise complete avoidance of the infant until the thoughts disappear.
Assure her intrusive thoughts can never pose risk and no further assessment is required.
explanations: Ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts with insight and compulsions are characteristic of OCD, but risk should still be assessed.
Correct: harm obsessions respond to ERP and serotonergic treatment, with proportionate risk assessment.
Insightful intrusive obsessions are not equivalent to delusional conviction or psychotic commands.
Total avoidance reinforces OCD and undermines functioning; safety assessment and graded ERP are more appropriate.
Risk assessment remains necessary, though unwanted ego-dystonic obsessions alone do not equal intent.
pearl: Unwanted ego-dystonic harm thoughts with reassurance seeking and avoidance suggest OCD; command hallucinations or delusional intent change urgency.
pivot: If the patient believes an external voice commands harming the infant or acts on the belief, consider psychotic disorder/postpartum psychosis and safeguarding.

steps: Clarify
Ask about insight, distress, feared urges versus wishes, compulsions, actual intent/plan, infant safety and mood symptoms.
Treat OCD
Offer structured CBT with ERP; consider SSRI when indicated, including perinatal risk–benefit discussion.
Support
Address avoidance, sleep, family reassurance cycles and monitor functioning and symptom severity.
management.safety: Avoid assuming all intrusive harm obsessions indicate dangerousness, but do not omit infant safety assessment.
management.local: Educational safety guide: confirm treatment and statutory reporting with your local specialist guidelines and safeguarding law.

stem: A 78-year-old with diarrhoea for three days has creatinine 250 µmol/L (baseline 95), dry mucosa, BP 92/58 mmHg, and minimal urine output. He takes ramipril and ibuprofen. No crackles, oedema or hydronephrosis. Urine microscopy is bland.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate initial approach?
options: Increase ramipril because ACE inhibitors improve renal blood flow during dehydration.
Begin immediate haemodialysis solely because creatinine has increased from baseline.
Treat with high-dose furosemide before examining volume status.
Ignore the AKI and repeat creatinine in two weeks once diarrhoea stops.
Give assessed isotonic fluid replacement, stop nephrotoxic contributors and monitor response and electrolytes.
explanations: ACE inhibition can worsen GFR during hypovolaemia and should be reviewed/withheld temporarily.
Dialysis depends on life-threatening complications and reversibility, not creatinine alone.
Diuresis may worsen hypovolaemic pre-renal AKI.
Hypoperfusion can progress to ATN and electrolyte complications without timely treatment.
Correct: history, hypotension and bland urine suggest pre-renal AKI from volume depletion and nephrotoxic medications.
pearl: Pre-renal AKI responds to restoring effective circulating volume; check for obstruction and medication contributors in every AKI.
pivot: If granular casts persist after perfusion restoration, consider evolving acute tubular injury rather than simply giving more fluid.

steps: Assess
ABC, orthostatic symptoms, mucosa, JVP, lungs, bladder scan and renal obstruction risk; UEC, K, bicarbonate and urine output.
Treat cause
Carefully titrated isotonic crystalloid with serial reassessment; temporarily pause NSAIDs and relevant BP/diuretic drugs.
Monitor
Strict fluid balance, repeat creatinine/electrolytes/ECG when needed, ensure urine output recovers.
Escalate
Nephrology for refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, overload, uraemic complications or persistent AKI.
management.safety: Small aliquots and frequent reassessment are especially important if concomitant heart failure exists.
management.local: Exam teaching framework. Confirm drug doses, contraindications and treatment thresholds with current local protocols and supervising teams.

stem: A 26-year-old G1P0 at 34+1 weeks reports that her baby has moved much less than usual since last night. She has no pain, fluid leak or bleeding. BP is normal and doppler confirms fetal heartbeat.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate next action?
options: Arrange same-day maternal/fetal assessment with CTG and risk-based ultrasound review, not simply reassurance from audible heartbeat.
Tell her to drink a sugary beverage and return after three days if movements remain reduced.
Arrange routine growth scan in six weeks and allow normal activities meanwhile.
Induce labour immediately without monitoring or assessing gestational risks.
Perform fetal scalp blood sampling in antenatal clinic.
explanations: Correct: reduced fetal movement warrants prompt surveillance; a heartbeat alone does not establish fetal wellbeing.
Home stimulation strategies must not delay formal assessment after concerning reduced movement.
Potential fetal compromise deserves assessment now, not at a routine future visit.
Delivery is not automatic for every isolated movement concern; test and individualise.
Fetal scalp testing is an intrapartum procedure, not an antenatal response to RFM.
pearl: Maternal perception of reduced movements is clinically important even when Doppler confirms a fetal heart rate.
pivot: If CTG is abnormal, expedite senior obstetric review, targeted ultrasound and possible birth depending on gestation and findings.

steps: Assess now
Review movement change, risk factors, BP, fetal heart and maternal symptoms; urgent CTG at viable gestation.
Investigate
Ultrasound for growth, fluid and Dopplers when indicated by risk/recurrent RFM or concerning CTG.
Communicate
Explain that a normal single assessment does not invalidate future concerns; return promptly if movement reduces again.
management.safety: Do not rely on home Dopplers to assess fetal wellbeing.
management.local: Clinical teaching only. Use the relevant maternity/neonatal/paediatric escalation pathway and current local drug/weight-based protocols.

stem: A 79-year-old with atrial fibrillation and inconsistent anticoagulation develops sudden severe diffuse abdominal pain. HR 116/min and lactate 4.2 mmol/L. Examination shows a soft abdomen with only mild tenderness despite extreme reported pain.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Arrange urgent CT angiography of mesenteric vessels with resuscitation and immediate vascular/general surgical consultation.
Start oral laxatives and wait for bowel sounds to return.
Perform routine colonoscopy before vascular imaging.
Reassure because the abdomen is not peritonitic.
Order plain abdominal radiograph and discharge if no free air appears.
explanations: Correct: acute mesenteric arterial embolism causes pain out of proportion and requires rapid vascular imaging and source-control planning.
Mechanical constipation cannot safely explain severe sudden pain and raised lactate in high-risk AF.
Colonoscopy delays diagnosis and risks perforation in possible ischaemic bowel.
Early mesenteric ischaemia can have a soft abdomen; peritonism is a late warning.
Plain film can be normal early and does not exclude mesenteric arterial occlusion.
pearl: Pain out of proportion to examination in AF is an acute mesenteric ischaemia alarm; the abdomen can be deceptively benign early.
pivot: Established peritonitis or bowel necrosis requires urgent laparotomy, not just endovascular restoration.

steps: Act immediately
IV access, fluid resuscitation, NPO, lactate/acid-base assessment, early antibiotics if threatened bowel, call surgery/vascular.
Image quickly
CTA arterial/portal phases despite renal concerns when high suspicion because delay threatens bowel survival.
Restore flow
Urgent anticoagulation when appropriate and specialist endovascular/open embolectomy or revascularisation.
Assess bowel viability
Laparotomy/resection when necrosis or peritonitis; repeat inspection if viability uncertain.
management.safety: An elevated lactate is a late/nonspecific sign; normal lactate does not exclude early mesenteric ischaemia.
management.local: Apply current hospital antibiotics, imaging, procedural and anticoagulation guidance with surgical and critical-care supervision.

context: Advanced psychiatry primary care and medication safety
stem: A 35-year-old is brought to ED after taking an unknown number of amitriptyline tablets. She is confused, hot, tachycardic at 140/min, hypotensive 88/50 mmHg with dry mucosa and urinary retention. ECG shows QRS duration 150 milliseconds.
ask: Which immediate treatment is MOST appropriate?
options: Give IV physostigmine for the anticholinergic symptoms without considering ECG findings.
Give IV flumazenil to reverse sedative co-ingestion before airway assessment.
Give an oral charcoal slurry without airway protection and observe.
Treat with IV sodium bicarbonate under ECG monitoring, resuscitation and toxicology/critical-care advice.
Give propranolol to control tachycardia despite hypotension.
explanations: Physostigmine is generally contraindicated in suspected TCA overdose with conduction delay/seizure risk.
Flumazenil risks seizures in mixed/TCA overdoses and is not treatment of sodium-channel blockade.
Airway status and cardiotoxicity are urgent; charcoal has aspiration risk and limited use depending time.
Correct: TCA sodium-channel blockade manifests with broad QRS and responds to bicarbonate alkalinisation/sodium loading.
Beta blockade may worsen circulatory collapse and does not reverse TCA cardiotoxicity.
pearl: TCA toxicity with wide QRS is sodium-channel blockade: IV sodium bicarbonate is a key antidotal therapy.
pivot: In isolated anticholinergic delirium without QRS abnormalities and after toxicology assessment, physostigmine may sometimes be considered.

steps: Resuscitate
ABCDE, protect airway, continuous ECG, IV access, glucose and electrolyte assessment; call poison centre/toxicology.
Treat cardiotoxicity
IV sodium bicarbonate boluses/infusion guided by QRS, BP and pH per toxicology protocol.
Address complications
Benzodiazepines for seizures, fluids/vasopressors as needed and monitor arrhythmias.
Observe
Repeat ECG/acid-base/electrolytes and psychiatric self-harm assessment once medically safe.
management.safety: Avoid class IA/IC antiarrhythmics, physostigmine and indiscriminate flumazenil in TCA toxicity.
management.local: Educational safety guide: confirm treatment and statutory reporting with your local specialist guidelines and safeguarding law.

stem: A 54-year-old with small-cell lung cancer has serum sodium 111 mmol/L and then a generalised tonic–clonic seizure. BP and oxygenation are currently maintained. Recent labs suggest SIADH and glucose is normal.
ask: Which initial treatment is MOST appropriate?
options: Fluid restriction alone until sodium rises by 1 mmol/L per day.
Give IV 3% hypertonic saline bolus per protocol with close sodium and neurological monitoring.
Give 2 L of free water intravenously to prevent central pontine myelinolysis.
Give desmopressin alone before any saline despite active seizures.
Wait for urine sodium and osmolality before treating the seizure.
explanations: A seizure from severe hyponatraemia is a medical emergency requiring immediate hypertonic saline.
Correct: severe symptomatic hyponatraemia needs rapid initial small rise to reverse cerebral oedema, then controlled correction.
Free water further lowers sodium and aggravates cerebral oedema.
Desmopressin may help prevent overcorrection in selected cases, but it is not the immediate rescue drug for hyponatraemic seizures.
Investigations are important but must not delay hypertonic saline when severe symptoms are present.
pearl: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia needs a controlled initial sodium rise, not normalisation; rapid total correction risks osmotic demyelination.
pivot: For mild/asymptomatic SIADH, fluid restriction and treatment of the cause may be first-line under monitoring.

steps: Resuscitate
Protect airway during seizure, check glucose and give anticonvulsant rescue if prolonged while treating underlying electrolyte emergency.
Correct acutely
Give measured 3% saline boluses per local severe symptomatic hyponatraemia guideline, reassess symptoms and sodium after each.
Prevent overshoot
Frequent sodium measurements and urine output checks, consider desmopressin/re-lowering strategy with specialist advice if rapid water diuresis occurs.
Treat cause
Review SIADH triggers and address tumour/medications after stabilisation.
management.safety: Do not aim for rapid normalisation; chronic hyponatraemia has high osmotic demyelination risk with overcorrection.
management.local: Exam teaching framework. Confirm drug doses, contraindications and treatment thresholds with current local protocols and supervising teams.

stem: A 5-year-old with no Hib immunisations has high fever, drooling, muffled voice and inspiratory stridor. He sits forward with chin extended and becomes distressed when staff approach. SpO2 is 94% in room air.
ask: What is the BEST immediate management?
options: Perform a vigorous tongue-depressor exam to visualise the epiglottis and confirm diagnosis.
Keep the child calm upright, summon experienced anaesthetic/ENT airway help and prepare controlled airway management.
Give nebulised salbutamol and perform spirometry before deciding about admission.
Transfer the child unaccompanied for lateral neck X-ray before calling for airway support.
Give oral penicillin and discharge after fever decreases.
explanations: Agitation and tongue-depressor examination can precipitate airway obstruction.
Correct: suspected epiglottitis is a dangerous upper-airway emergency managed with expert help and minimal distress.
Salbutamol does not resolve supraglottic swelling; spirometry is inappropriate.
Imaging should not delay or jeopardise airway rescue; unnecessary transport is risky.
Oral outpatient treatment is unsafe; airway and IV antimicrobial management are urgent.
pearl: Drooling, tripod positioning, toxic appearance and muffled voice suggest supraglottitis rather than uncomplicated croup.
pivot: Barking cough with stridor but no drooling/toxic features suggests viral croup where dexamethasone/nebulised adrenaline are useful.

steps: Do not agitate
Keep sitting position and parent nearby; monitor non-invasively and avoid throat examinations.
Call airway team
Anaesthesia, ENT, paediatrics and theatre support; prepare controlled airway securing by experienced clinician.
Treat infection
Once airway safe, blood cultures if feasible and IV antibiotics per local epiglottitis guideline.
Observe
High-acuity monitoring for deterioration; evaluate immunisation status once recovered.
management.safety: Avoid attempts at IV access or imaging if they dangerously upset the child before expert airway control.
management.local: Clinical teaching only. Use the relevant maternity/neonatal/paediatric escalation pathway and current local drug/weight-based protocols.

stem: A 67-year-old with left iliac fossa pain and fever has CT-confirmed sigmoid diverticulitis with a 5.2 cm pericolic abscess. She is haemodynamically stable with no diffuse peritonitis, but WCC is 18 × 10^9/L.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Discharge on analgesia alone because most diverticulitis is self-limiting.
Proceed to emergency Hartmann procedure immediately irrespective of stability or drainage feasibility.
Give oral laxatives and high fibre immediately to improve colonic transit.
Admit for IV antibiotics and surgical review with image-guided abscess drainage assessment.
Start IV corticosteroids as sole treatment for inflammatory colonic disease.
explanations: A sizeable abscess is complicated diverticulitis and needs active inpatient assessment.
Surgery may be required for diffuse peritonitis or failed non-operative treatment but is not automatic for stable contained abscess.
Active diverticulitis with abscess is not managed by stimulant bowel opening.
Correct: large accessible abscesses generally benefit from percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics where feasible.
Steroids increase infection risk and do not drain an abscess.
pearl: Size and accessibility of diverticular abscess guide drainage; physiological stability and peritonitis determine surgical urgency.
pivot: If generalised purulent/faecal peritonitis or shock develops, operative source control becomes urgent.

steps: Assess
NPO initially as needed, IV fluids, analgesia, cultures for sepsis and assess CT for perforation extent.
Treat infection
IV antibiotics active against enteric Gram-negative and anaerobic bacteria, surgical team involvement.
Drain if feasible
IR evaluation for percutaneous drain of larger accessible collection; surgery if not drainable or clinical deterioration.
Recover and follow
Tailor antibiotics to culture, repeat imaging for poor response and plan subsequent bowel assessment per local recommendations.
management.safety: Do not perform colonoscopy during the acute perforated/infected phase.
management.local: Apply current hospital antibiotics, imaging, procedural and anticoagulation guidance with surgical and critical-care supervision.

context: Advanced psychiatry primary care and medication safety
stem: A 30-year-old at 17 weeks gestation has eight weeks of pervasive low mood, anhedonia, marked insomnia and poor oral intake. She previously responded well to sertraline but stopped it when pregnant. She denies current suicidal plans but finds working and self-care difficult.
ask: Which management is MOST appropriate?
options: Offer collaborative perinatal mental health assessment, psychological therapy and discuss restarting an effective antidepressant after risk–benefit review.
Withhold all effective depression treatment until after delivery because medications are universally teratogenic.
Use only a sedative hypnotic for months without treating depressed mood.
Require inpatient admission in every pregnant person who reports any depressive symptom.
Prescribe valproate as first-line because it has strong mood stabilisation effects.
explanations: Correct: significant antenatal depression warrants active treatment; both untreated illness and medication risks should be discussed individually.
Untreated depression can have substantial maternal and fetal consequences; many treatments are considered after individual assessment.
Sedation alone does not adequately treat MDD and carries its own risks.
Admission is based on severity and safety, not pregnancy or depression alone.
Valproate is not first-line for unipolar depression and poses substantial teratogenic risk.
pearl: Treating antenatal depression is shared decision-making: severity, prior response, maternal safety and fetal exposure all matter.
pivot: Suicidal intent, psychosis, inability to eat/drink or severe self-neglect require urgent specialist assessment and possible admission.

steps: Assess safety and severity
Detailed suicidality/self-harm, psychosis, nutrition, substance use, functioning and supports; exclude thyroid/anaemia if indicated.
Plan treatment
Offer CBT/interpersonal therapy and consider restarting previously effective SSRI with perinatal psychiatry/obstetric input.
Monitor
Early follow-up for symptom response, side effects, sleep, nutrition and postpartum relapse risk.
Coordinate
Communicate with GP, obstetrics and mental health services and plan postnatal support.
management.safety: Do not abruptly discontinue effective psychiatric medication in pregnancy without discussing relapse and withdrawal risks.
management.local: Educational safety guide: confirm treatment and statutory reporting with your local specialist guidelines and safeguarding law.

stem: A 48-year-old taking long-term prednisolone for vasculitis has vomiting, fever and profound lethargy. He could not take steroids for 48 hours. BP 76/42 mmHg, glucose 3.1 mmol/L, Na 126 mmol/L and K 5.7 mmol/L.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Give IV hydrocortisone immediately plus isotonic fluids and dextrose as needed; obtain cultures/treat trigger.
Perform a standard ACTH stimulation test and wait for results before any steroids.
Start high-dose mineralocorticoid alone without glucocorticoid treatment.
Stop all steroids and observe electrolytes until infection resolves.
Give only ondansetron and oral electrolyte solution because vomiting causes all findings.
explanations: Correct: likely adrenal crisis requires emergency parenteral glucocorticoids and haemodynamic/glucose support.
Testing should not delay steroids in adrenal crisis; cortisol/ACTH can be sampled first if it will not delay.
Acute cortisol deficiency is life-threatening; mineralocorticoid alone will not treat shock.
This worsens adrenal insufficiency and potentially causes cardiovascular collapse.
Shock, hypoglycaemia and steroid interruption suggest endocrine emergency beyond simple gastroenteritis.
pearl: Treat suspected adrenal crisis immediately with parenteral hydrocortisone and fluids; do not await endocrine confirmation.
pivot: If stable and undergoing elective steroid dose reduction, investigate HPA-axis recovery without crisis dosing.

steps: First minutes
ABCDE, urgent IV access, check glucose and electrolytes, sample cortisol/ACTH only if no delay; call senior.
Replace cortisol
Give IV hydrocortisone emergency dose and ongoing replacement per local adrenal-crisis protocol.
Resuscitate
Isotonic saline with reassessment; correct hypoglycaemia with IV dextrose and address infection/source.
Plan
Educate sick-day dosing, emergency injection kit and endocrine follow-up when recovered.
management.safety: Monitor potassium, fluid overload and infection; do not miss sepsis coexisting with adrenal crisis.
management.local: Exam teaching framework. Confirm drug doses, contraindications and treatment thresholds with current local protocols and supervising teams.

stem: A term newborn at 4 days becomes pale and poorly feeding. Femoral pulses are very weak, upper-limb BP 94/56 mmHg, lower-limb BP 48/30 mmHg, capillary refill 5 seconds, lactate 7 mmol/L. Pulse oximetry is 95% in the right hand.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Give a standard bolus of loop diuretic and observe for improved leg perfusion.
Administer oral propranolol to lower right-arm systolic pressure to match legs.
Start prostaglandin E1 infusion with neonatal cardiac/ICU consultation and supportive resuscitation.
Wait for echocardiography tomorrow because normal right-hand saturation excludes congenital heart disease.
Give inhaled nitric oxide as sole therapy for presumed persistent pulmonary hypertension.
explanations: Poor systemic perfusion from duct closure is not treated by diuresis; it may worsen shock.
Beta blockade is inappropriate in neonatal shock from possible critical coarctation.
Correct: critical coarctation may be duct-dependent for systemic blood flow; reopening the ductus buys time for intervention.
Saturation may be near-normal in systemic duct-dependent lesions; clinical perfusion signs demand urgent action.
Pulmonary vasodilation does not fix mechanical aortic arch obstruction causing lower-body hypoperfusion.
pearl: Duct-dependent systemic lesions can cause shock as the PDA closes, often with weak femoral pulses and arm–leg BP gradient.
pivot: If a neonate is severely cyanosed with duct-dependent pulmonary blood flow, prostaglandin also helps by maintaining PDA, but the physiology differs.

steps: Stabilise
Neonatal resuscitation/transport team, ABC, glucose, temperature, blood gas and lactate monitoring, IV access.
Reopen duct
Commence PGE1 (alprostadil) per neonatal cardiac protocol; prepare for possible apnoea and assisted ventilation.
Confirm lesion
Urgent echocardiography, four-limb BP/pulses, pre/postductal saturations and cardiology/heart surgery planning.
Manage shock
Cautious perfusion support and monitor lactate, urine output and acid-base.
management.safety: PGE1 can cause apnoea and hypotension; monitor in a setting prepared to ventilate.
management.local: Clinical teaching only. Use the relevant maternity/neonatal/paediatric escalation pathway and current local drug/weight-based protocols.

stem: A 58-year-old woman develops unilateral left calf swelling, discomfort and 3 cm greater circumference after a ten-hour flight. She is afebrile, no skin break or erythema, HR 84/min, and no dyspnoea. Wells assessment indicates DVT likely.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate next investigation?
options: Begin oral flucloxacillin and reassess the calf after seven days.
Arrange urgent compression ultrasonography, with anticoagulation timing guided by delay and bleeding risk.
Obtain arterial Doppler for peripheral arterial disease as first-line.
Use a D-dimer alone to exclude DVT despite a high clinical probability.
Order CT pulmonary angiography in every swollen leg even without PE symptoms.
explanations: Cellulitis is less consistent without erythema/fever; a likely DVT requires specific assessment.
Correct: ultrasound tests for proximal DVT; empiric anticoagulation is considered when testing is delayed and safe.
PAD causes ischaemia/claudication rather than acute venous swelling after prolonged travel.
With high pre-test probability, negative D-dimer is less reliable than definitive imaging.
Routine CTPA is not indicated without symptoms or signs suggesting PE.
pearl: A structured DVT probability score guides D-dimer and ultrasound; do not use D-dimer as the sole test in likely DVT.
pivot: If chest pain, collapse or hypoxaemia occurs, assess urgently for concurrent PE.

steps: Assess risk
Wells score, bleeding risk, pregnancy status and contraindications to anticoagulation.
Image
Compression ultrasound; repeat scan when indicated if initial study negative and clinical suspicion persists.
Treat confirmed DVT
Start anticoagulation according to renal function, bleeding risk and pregnancy status; educate on PE warning signs.
management.safety: Recent surgery, active bleeding or pregnancy alters drug and imaging choices.
management.local: Apply current hospital antibiotics, imaging, procedural and anticoagulation guidance with surgical and critical-care supervision.

skill: Symptomatic colorectal cancer / screening vs diagnosis
context: Advanced psychiatry primary care and medication safety
stem: A 58-year-old man reports new change in bowel habit, fatigue, 7 kg unintended weight loss and iron-deficiency anaemia (Hb 96 g/L, ferritin 7 µg/L). He asks for a home FIT because his last screening FIT was negative 15 months ago.
ask: What is the BEST investigation strategy?
options: Repeat screening FIT in two years because the previous result was negative.
Treat iron deficiency with tablets alone and ignore the cause if Hb rises.
Offer urgent diagnostic colonoscopy / appropriate lower GI pathway rather than relying on the old screening FIT.
Order serum carcinoembryonic antigen alone because it is a sensitive diagnostic screening test.
Arrange routine abdominal X-ray and discharge if it is normal.
explanations: Screening tests are for asymptomatic average-risk populations; alarm symptoms need diagnostic assessment.
Iron replacement does not investigate potentially serious colorectal blood loss.
Correct: symptomatic iron-deficiency anaemia and weight loss require direct investigation for malignancy.
CEA is not suitable as a stand-alone diagnostic test for colorectal cancer.
Plain radiography cannot exclude colorectal cancer.
pearl: A negative FIT does not overrule red-flag symptoms or unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia: investigation is diagnostic, not screening.
pivot: In an asymptomatic average-risk adult, programme-based FIT screening remains appropriate at recommended intervals.

steps: Assess
History incl bleeding, weight loss, family history, bowel change, abdominal/rectal examination and FBC/iron studies.
Investigate
Urgent diagnostic colonoscopy or locally indicated CT colonography if colonoscopy unavailable/contraindicated.
Treat concurrent problems
Manage iron deficiency and symptoms while investigating, not instead of it.
Follow up
Ensure referral is received, results acted on and safety net if obstruction/bleeding develops.
management.safety: Do not use CEA or prior normal FIT to dismiss symptomatic cancer risk.
management.local: Educational safety guide: confirm treatment and statutory reporting with your local specialist guidelines and safeguarding law.

stem: A 37-year-old with known untreated Graves disease develops temperature 40.0 °C, HR 160/min irregularly irregular, vomiting, agitation and pulmonary congestion after pneumonia. Free T4 is markedly elevated and TSH suppressed.
ask: Which regimen BEST addresses thyroid storm after immediate resuscitation?
options: Start iodine solution first, followed by thionamide the next day.
Treat with aspirin and discharge when fever falls.
Give a beta blocker alone and rely on endogenous thyroid hormone clearance.
Use appropriately monitored beta blockade, thionamide then iodine after an interval, glucocorticoid and treatment of trigger.
Perform immediate elective radioiodine ablation before stabilisation.
explanations: Iodine before blocking new hormone synthesis can worsen hormone production; sequence matters.
Aspirin may increase free thyroid hormone and discharge is unsafe in multi-organ thyrotoxic crisis.
Beta blockade controls symptoms but not synthesis/release or systemic illness; comprehensive treatment is needed.
Correct: multimodal treatment reduces adrenergic activity, synthesis, release, peripheral conversion and treats precipitant.
Radioiodine does not act promptly and is not acute management of storm.
pearl: Thyroid storm is a clinical emergency; treat synthesis (thionamide) before iodine and use steroids plus supportive care.
pivot: If uncomplicated hyperthyroidism without fever/organ dysfunction, outpatient antithyroid treatment and monitoring may be possible.

steps: Critical-care assessment
ECG, BP, fluids with careful overload assessment, oxygen when indicated, cooling, paracetamol, trigger cultures/antibiotics.
Control adrenergic drive
Beta blocker selected for cardiac function and haemodynamics (short-acting agent if unstable/high risk).
Block thyroid hormone
Thionamide, then iodine after appropriate interval, plus glucocorticoid per endocrinology protocol.
Monitor
Arrhythmias, heart failure, liver function, temperature and treatment adverse effects.
management.safety: Aggressive beta blockade can collapse patients with cardiogenic shock or severe thyrotoxic cardiomyopathy; specialist titration is crucial.
management.local: Exam teaching framework. Confirm drug doses, contraindications and treatment thresholds with current local protocols and supervising teams.

stem: A previously healthy 20-month-old develops a generalized convulsion during a viral illness. The seizure has continued for 7 minutes in ED. He is cyanotic around the mouth with SpO2 88% and no vascular access.
ask: What is the BEST next intervention?
options: Wait until the seizure reaches 30 minutes before treating it.
Give oral paracetamol and reassure the parents that antipyretics stop febrile seizures.
Perform CT head before administering any anticonvulsant.
Give benzodiazepine rescue by an available non-IV route with airway support and check glucose.
Commence long-term prophylactic sodium valproate before checking the airway.
explanations: A convulsion lasting at least 5 minutes is unlikely to stop promptly and merits emergency treatment.
Antipyretics do not terminate an ongoing seizure and do not reliably prevent recurrence.
Imaging should not delay airway support or rescue treatment during active status.
Correct: treat convulsive seizure >=5 min immediately with appropriately dosed benzodiazepine via buccal/intranasal/IM route per protocol.
Maintenance antiepileptics are not first-line for an acute convulsive seizure in a toddler.
pearl: A seizure reaching five minutes is treated as early convulsive status epilepticus; airway, glucose and benzodiazepine rescue run together.
pivot: A typical brief simple febrile seizure that has stopped and normalises may need observation and parent education rather than routine long-term antiepileptics.

steps: ABCDE
Protect from injury, position airway, oxygen as needed, check bedside glucose and vital signs; time seizure.
Stop seizure
Give an appropriate non-IV benzodiazepine rescue when IV unavailable per age/weight policy; reassess and follow escalation sequence if persistent.
Find fever source
After seizure stops, assess meningitis/sepsis red flags, hydration, focused history and recurrence risks.
Communicate
Explain seizure first aid, return precautions and discharge criteria if appropriate.
management.safety: Repeated benzodiazepines can depress breathing; follow dose limits and prepare bag-mask ventilation.
management.local: Clinical teaching only. Use the relevant maternity/neonatal/paediatric escalation pathway and current local drug/weight-based protocols.

stem: A 51-year-old has fever 39.3 °C, left flank pain, BP 90/54 mmHg and pyuria. CT shows a 9 mm proximal ureteric stone with marked hydronephrosis. Lactate is 3.4 mmol/L.
ask: What is the BEST urgent management?
options: Prescribe oral trimethoprim and wait for stone passage at home.
Arrange elective lithotripsy in six weeks without early antibiotics.
Begin IV antibiotics/resuscitation and organise urgent ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy.
Give IV furosemide to increase urinary flow against the ureteric obstruction.
Perform forceful retrograde stone manipulation before treating septic shock.
explanations: Infected obstructed system with sepsis is life-threatening and unlikely to clear with oral therapy alone.
Definitive stone removal is delayed until sepsis controlled, but immediate drainage and antibiotics are essential.
Correct: antibiotic therapy cannot fully sterilise an obstructed infected collecting system without source control.
Diuresis risks worsening hydronephrosis and does not relieve mechanical blockage.
Acute sepsis requires antibiotics and decompression with controlled urologic intervention, not unprepared definitive stone extraction.
pearl: An infected obstructed kidney is a true source-control emergency: drain first, remove the stone later.
pivot: An uncomplicated, afebrile small ureteric stone without infection may pass with analgesia and outpatient follow-up.

steps: Sepsis response
ABCDE, IV cultures, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, fluid resuscitation and BP monitoring.
Drain urgently
Early urology/IR collaboration for ureteric stent or nephrostomy.
Track response
Urine output, creatinine, lactate, temperature, blood/urine culture guidance.
Plan definitive therapy
Stone clearance after infection and sepsis are controlled.
management.safety: Do not delay decompression until antibiotics have 'worked' in obstructive sepsis.
management.local: Apply current hospital antibiotics, imaging, procedural and anticoagulation guidance with surgical and critical-care supervision.

context: Advanced psychiatry primary care and medication safety
stem: A 15-year-old discloses to a GP that an adult neighbour forced sexual contact yesterday. She is frightened, asks that her caregiver not be informed and does not want police involvement. She is physically stable but distressed.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate initial clinical response?
options: Promise absolute secrecy regardless of statutory child-protection duties.
Demand a full detailed recount before arranging any medical care.
Arrange a public discussion with the caregiver and alleged perpetrator to clarify events.
Provide trauma-informed care, immediate safety assessment, time-sensitive medical/forensic options and explain reporting obligations clearly.
Dismiss the disclosure if no visible injuries are present.
explanations: Clinicians must explain confidentiality limits, especially where child sexual abuse triggers mandatory safeguarding reporting.
Repeated intrusive questioning can retraumatise and compromise forensic interview processes.
Confrontation jeopardises privacy, safety and evidence, and can escalate risk.
Correct: patient-centred response balances autonomy, emergency care and child-protection law.
Sexual assault often leaves no external injury; absence of physical signs does not invalidate disclosure.
pearl: In adolescent assault disclosure, first ensure safety and explain confidentiality honestly; medical/forensic and safeguarding pathways are time-sensitive.
pivot: For a competent adult who discloses assault, reporting requirements and consent differ; check local law and the patient's wishes.

steps: Ensure safety
Private, non-judgmental interview and assess imminent danger, self-harm risk, safe supports and capacity/consent for care.
Medical care
Offer specialist sexual assault service promptly for forensic evidence, STI prophylaxis/testing, pregnancy risk/emergency contraception, and injury care.
Safeguard and document
Explain mandatory child-protection obligations and consent boundaries; record facts in the patient's own words, avoid unnecessary repeated questioning.
Follow-up
Trauma-focused psychological support, safe contact method and follow-up care coordination.
management.safety: Reporting laws vary; do not promise secrecy that conflicts with child protection duties.
management.local: Educational safety guide: confirm treatment and statutory reporting with your local specialist guidelines and safeguarding law.

stem: A 70-year-old with COPD exacerbation has received inhaled bronchodilators, corticosteroid and controlled oxygen. ABG on titrated oxygen: pH 7.26, PaCO2 78 mmHg, PaO2 65 mmHg. He is awake, cooperative, protecting airway, with moderate work of breathing.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate next respiratory intervention?
options: Increase oxygen to 100% by non-rebreather irrespective of saturation.
Give repeated sedative doses to suppress respiratory effort without further review.
Commence monitored non-invasive ventilation with targeted oxygen and early reassessment of clinical state and ABG.
Intubate immediately in every hypercapnic COPD patient irrespective of NIV suitability.
Discharge on oral antibiotics because the PaO2 is above 60 mmHg.
explanations: Uncontrolled high oxygen can worsen hypercapnia and does not directly support ventilation.
Sedatives may precipitate hypoventilation and loss of airway protection.
Correct: persistent hypercapnic respiratory acidosis with suitable consciousness/airway makes NIV an evidence-based intervention.
Intubation is needed if NIV contraindicated or failing; selected patients benefit from trial of NIV.
Acidaemic hypercapnic respiratory failure needs inpatient ventilatory support and monitoring.
pearl: NIV is indicated for selected COPD exacerbations with persistent acute hypercapnic respiratory acidosis despite initial treatment.
pivot: If drowsy, unable to protect airway, severely unstable or rapidly deteriorating, invasive ventilation may be safer.

steps: Continue baseline care
Controlled oxygen usually aiming 88–92% unless individually indicated, bronchodilators, steroids and antibiotics if criteria met.
Start NIV
Begin monitored bilevel NIV in appropriate unit; check mask fit, comfort, patient synchrony and contraindications.
Reassess early
Repeat ABG and clinical work of breathing within protocol times; monitor aspiration, hypotension and deterioration.
Escalate
Critical care/intubation if worsening pH, consciousness, secretion burden or NIV intolerance.
management.safety: Titrate oxygen to physiologic need; avoid indiscriminate high-concentration oxygen in CO2 retainers.
management.local: Exam teaching framework. Confirm drug doses, contraindications and treatment thresholds with current local protocols and supervising teams.

stem: A 7-year-old has palpable purpura over legs and buttocks, ankle pain and mild colicky abdominal discomfort. Platelet count is normal. Urinalysis has 1+ blood but no protein; BP and renal function are normal.
ask: Which follow-up approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Reassure and discharge with no further testing because skin rash is self-limiting.
Give immediate high-dose IV immunosuppression to all affected children.
Request skin biopsy routinely before assessing urine or blood pressure.
Start prophylactic anticoagulation because palpable purpura indicates thrombosis.
Provide supportive symptom care with scheduled BP and urine protein/blood checks and renal referral if abnormalities progress.
explanations: Renal involvement may develop after rash onset and warrants serial urinalysis/BP even when initially mild.
Most mild IgA vasculitis is self-limiting; treatment depends on organ severity, not rash alone.
Classic palpable purpura with normal platelets is a clinical diagnosis; renal surveillance is more important.
IgA vasculitis is small-vessel inflammation, not an indication for routine anticoagulation.
Correct: monitor for delayed nephritis, hypertension and significant proteinuria.
pearl: IgA vasculitis is a systemic small-vessel vasculitis; the long-term risk is renal, not the rash.
pivot: If significant proteinuria, impaired eGFR or hypertension develops, prompt nephrology evaluation and kidney-directed treatment are needed.

steps: Assess severity
BP, urine dip/UPCR if indicated, renal function, abdominal exam for intussusception, testicular pain and joint symptoms.
Support
Analgesia and hydration; avoid NSAIDs if renal impairment or GI bleeding; treat severe abdominal/joint symptoms under paediatric advice.
Follow renal status
Document a scheduled serial BP/urine surveillance plan over subsequent months.
Escalate
Nephrology for persistent/progressive proteinuria, hypertension or renal dysfunction; ED for GI bleeding/severe pain.
management.safety: Absence of proteinuria on day one does not end renal surveillance.
management.local: Clinical teaching only. Use the relevant maternity/neonatal/paediatric escalation pathway and current local drug/weight-based protocols.

stem: A 45-year-old reports a sudden 'worst-ever' thunderclap headache that peaked within seconds 13 hours ago, with vomiting and neck pain. He is alert with normal neurological examination. Non-contrast CT head done now is reported normal.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Discharge because any negative CT excludes subarachnoid haemorrhage at all times.
Start oral migraine therapy and defer further evaluation for a week.
Administer fibrinolysis for presumed cerebral thrombosis.
Arrange emergency LP and/or vascular imaging according to the local SAH pathway after senior discussion.
Repeat CT in a month because the blood becomes more conspicuous with time.
explanations: CT sensitivity is time dependent and a delayed negative CT may not reliably exclude SAH.
Thunderclap onset with meningism is a high-risk red flag; further SAH assessment is required.
Fibrinolysis is dangerous if haemorrhage is present and no thrombotic diagnosis is established.
Correct: after >6 hours, a negative CT alone may be insufficient; further diagnostic testing is appropriate.
Blood becomes less visible over time; waiting is unsafe.
pearl: A thunderclap headache requires SAH exclusion even with normal neurological examination, especially when CT is delayed beyond six hours.
pivot: For CT within six hours with high-quality scan and expert reading, some guidelines allow exclusion without LP in selected patients.

steps: Assess
ABC, BP, neurological exam, analgesia and avoid anticoagulation until bleed excluded.
Investigate safely
Senior ED/neurology discussion, LP timing/CSF xanthochromia or CTA pathway depending local SAH algorithm.
If confirmed
Urgent neurosurgical transfer, BP/complication management and aneurysm treatment.
management.safety: LP is contraindicated in selected raised-ICP or coagulopathy situations; choose further tests with specialist input.
management.local: Apply current hospital antibiotics, imaging, procedural and anticoagulation guidance with surgical and critical-care supervision.

context: Advanced psychiatry primary care and medication safety
stem: An 82-year-old with non-valvular AF, previous TIA, hypertension and diabetes is not anticoagulated because he fell twice last year without major injury. BP is controlled and renal function is stable. He has no active bleeding.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate discussion?
options: Recommend aspirin alone because any fall risk contraindicates all oral anticoagulation.
Withhold all antithrombotic treatment until he is free of falls for 12 months.
Start dual antiplatelet therapy rather than anticoagulation irrespective of bleeding risk.
Give full-dose anticoagulant without checking kidney function, weight, interactions or patient preference.
Discuss an oral anticoagulant with individualised bleeding/falls mitigation and correct dose selection.
explanations: Aspirin is not an effective equivalent substitute for AF stroke prevention in high-risk patients.
Falls risk alone usually does not outweigh high thromboembolic risk; modifiable contributors should be addressed.
Dual antiplatelets are generally less effective and still cause bleeding; not routine AF stroke prevention.
